Crafted byAdithya N Raj
Full campaign · 54 tasks × 7 models · 378 of 378 runs finished · 378 scored · 125 hours of generation · updated 24 Nov 2026

Which local model builds the best software?

Seven Qwen3.8 builds, served from one RTX 5090, each worked alone through the same 54 tasks: games and 3D worlds, SVG and shaders, web apps and extensions, C++, Rust and Go, refactors and bug hunts, LaTeX papers and research write-ups. Every result is rebuilt, run, screenshotted and tested by hand, then scored out of 10.

M4 leads on the 54 tasks that every model has a score for (8.98), ahead of M7 (8.89), close enough that the two are effectively tied. Every run was regraded on 18 Nov 2026 on Visual, Prompt following, Output, Creativity and Code, with points taken off for visual errors and bugs. The owner then played and rated every game, 3D, sound and design task by hand (cards marked Rated by the owner); the code-only tasks keep my scores. The X4 DevOps runs of M4, M5 and M6 are scored from their code and their own run logs, because rerunning them needs Docker Desktop. The hallucination study covers all builds, including the server-guardrail incident.

P2Flight combat simulator (Godot + Blender)

Best: M7 8.3
The task prompt the models received
Design and create a flight combat simulator game. The game must feature 3d graphics in any style you choose.

A Start Screen that allows the user to select the plane they will use. The user may select from three potential options as follows: A Fighter Jet, A Propeller Plane, An option of your choosing.

Each Plane must have realistic limitations on its performance, which should also be displayed graphically on the plane selection screen.

Once the plane is selected and the game started, there will be a dynamic number of opposing planes the user can engage in a dogfight with. There MUST be visible ammunition traces, as well as functional damage implementation for both enemy and player planes.

If the player defeats all enemy planes in a round, the level repeats with increased difficulty. If the player loses, the plane they are in becomes uncontrollable and falls to the ground, returning them to the home screen following a 2 second black screen.

You must use blender and godot for this. Both are installed on the system.

Full evaluation note

Re-run. M1's first P2 ran before the preview tool existed (kept in runs/_superseded/…-P2-flight-combat-pre-preview-* with notes and media; scored 9/9/5/7/8). This re-run hit the 90-min cap. The watchdog released one hung Godot probe call at 23:33 and escalated at 23:34 (≈ 5 min lost; first live use of the escalation).

My verification (scratch copy, Blender 4.2.23, Godot 4.2.2)

  • blender --background --python build_planes.py rebuilds all three GLBs (rc 0).

  • Menu (windowed): "STRATA STRIKE — select your aircraft": VF-27 Ghostfire (supersonic jet), PT-9 Sailor (propeller dogfighter), AH-41 Mantis (attack helicopter) with stat bars (speed/accel/turn/fire/armor) and spec lines (620 / 262 / 185 kt, guns, hull). All three cards show the same jet thumbnail.

  • Ground shader fails to compile: the terrain shader uses WORLD_POSITION and writes COLOR in a spatial fragment shader (invalid in Godot 4), so the terrain never renders — every flight shot is pale sky with flat cloud discs and no ground (Godot prints the failing shader source, not an ERROR: line, so the launcher's error count shows 0).

  • Real play (my input script: click LAUNCH, throttle, hold Space/LMB, turn): round 1 starts with 4 enemies; firing works (ammo 100 → 95 → 60 → 32); about 12 s in the plane hits the invisible ground (hull still 100) and the game returns to the menu — the death/return path works, but the player crashes into terrain they cannot see.

  • --demo / --autostart autopilot: flies for 60 s without firing (ammo stays 100) though one hostile was lost in an autostart run ("HOSTILES 3/4").

  • Its test/test_harness.tscn is stale: crashes in _ready (global_position on a freed node).

  • Code has tracers (FX.spawn_tracer, tracer.gd applying take_damage to enemies and player), round progression and a death sequence; I did not see enemy hits on the player within my runs.

Full campaign, M3 leg.

  • Ran to the 90-min cap (242 turns). It was still polishing the explosion effect at the end, but the game itself was complete.

  • It left a lot of clutter in the project: tools/probe/ with 25 probe scripts, tools/.orig_scripts/ backups, an empty nul file, and a tools/probe.gd that fails to parse under Godot 4.2.

  • Debug hooks are still in the game: in demo or headless mode it prints status lines, and between frames 440 and 540 it spawns explosions in front of the camera.

My verification (scratch copy; Blender 4.2.23, Godot 4.2.2, the versions it used)

  • blender --background --python tools/make_models.py rebuilds the three GLBs (rc 0, byte-identical sizes; relative output path).

  • godot --headless --import: the only errors come from the leftover tools/probe.gd.

  • Plane-select screen (native_eval.py, quiet window; -menu-end.png): "STRATA DOGFIGHT — select your aircraft".
    • Three cards, each with a rotating 3D model of its Blender plane: FALCON XF-9 (jet), OSPREY PT-47 (propeller) and DREADNOUGHT HB-7 (gunship).
    • Each card shows real limits (top speed 880 / 462 / 330 km/h, hull, rounds per second, stall speed 352 / 154 / 121 km/h) and stat bars for speed, agility, firepower, durability and ammo.
    • Layout flaw: each card's one-line description runs past the card edge and is cut off.

  • Gameplay (-- demo, autopilot, 45 s; -sheet.png, -8s.png):

    • HUD shows hull and ammo bars, round, hostiles, score, speed and throttle.
    • 3 enemy planes; red enemy tracers are visible.
    • The scene is pale and washed-out by heavy haze, with flat-topped cone mountains and white cloud blobs.
    • The autopilot killed nothing in 45 s.
    • Log: 1 shader compile error (Unknown identifier 'world') and 126 "!is_inside_tree" errors from get_global_transform.

  • Own headless probe (_delete/eval-scratch/p2-m3/work/probe_waves.gd, run as an autoload; the player is kept alive and enemies are destroyed through the game's own damage function):

    • Rounds escalate: round 1 has 3 enemies (HP 42, aim error 0.095), round 2 has 4 (51), round 3 has 5 (60), round 4 has 6 (69) and round 5 has 7 (78, aim error 0.047).
    • Enemy speed and gun damage also rise per round.
    • Then the player is killed: "HULL LOST — AIRFRAME UNCONTROLLABLE". Input is ignored while the plane spirals down from 150 m for 7 s.
    • Then comes a black screen, and after 2.3 s the game returns to the home screen.
    • On return, start_screen reports 3 script errors setting the environment on a null world (seen headless; it may not happen in a window).

  • Code: a flight model with stall below the minimum speed, ground collision damage, pooled bullets with segment hit-tests, and a separate aim error per round.

Full evaluation note

Full campaign, M3 leg. 73 min of the 90-min cap, 328 turns, 326K tokens; it used preview heavily (~200 mentions). Most of the session went on finding its own rendering bugs. Its summary lists them:

  • the world was drawn without glBegin/glEnd, so none of it appeared;
  • GDI text was invisible over the GL buffer, so it switched to wglUseFontBitmaps;
  • the cockpit was drawn over the eye point.

My verification (scratch copy)

  • Rebuilt with its command (Strawberry g++ -O2 -Wall rally.cpp -lopengl32 -lgdi32 -luser32): 0 errors, 0 warnings.
  • Drove it quietly with native_eval.py: Enter, W 6 s, then A and D while holding W, then Esc, Esc. Window "GRAN RALLY - Low-Poly Rally", 0 error lines.
    • Menu: "GRAN RALLY — LOW-POLY RALLY SINCE 1994", ▶ START RALLY / QUIT with a highlight bar, "WASD DRIVE · ESC MENU", checkered borders, over a live, darkened view of the track with pines and props.
    • In game: first-person cockpit with A-pillars, dashboard and a steering wheel that visibly rotates with A/D. Speed readout (0 → 57 km/h). Road with lane markings on the start straight.
    • But the dashboard and roof fill the upper two thirds of the screen. The road shows only in a strip at the bottom, so the scenery that is drawn (trees, mountains, clouds) is barely visible while driving.
    • Driving straight leaves the road within ~4 s ("OFF ROAD", the car slows to 16 → 0 km/h). After that the view is flat green grass under the dashboard.
    • Esc brings the menu back over the stage, and Esc again resumes.
  • Track: a closed spline with height (trackH), with the terrain blended into rolling hills (hillsAt), so it has elevation. There is no lap timer or other objective; the HUD is the speed and "ESC MENU", the latter low-contrast and clipped at the top right.

Full evaluation note

Full campaign, M3 leg. 26 min of the 45-min cap; it used preview about 60 times, always on demo.html. The run's one "outside write", B:\Research\[owner folder] (a git clone created at 01:54), is not mentioned anywhere in the transcript; it is the owner's own activity.

My verification

  • capture.mjs --mode game on index.html (20 s): 0 failed requests but 6 page errors: "Cannot access 'p' before initialization".

  • Game-breaking bug. AudioFX.groan(p) reads const t=…, p=p||1, which re-declares the parameter, so it throws whenever the audio context exists. The audio context is created by the player's first click, which is the click that starts the game. spawnZombie() calls groan after it has added the zombie but before return true, so wavePending is never decremented.

    • Wave 1 therefore never ends: zombies keep spawning to the cap. My probe killed 271 zombies, and the game stayed on wave 1 with the train "away".
    • The train, wave 2 and every later wave are unreachable in real play.
    • Its own checks used demo.html, which never clicks, so audio stayed off and the bug never fired.

  • Patched copy (_delete/eval-scratch/p4-m3/, only p=p||1 turned into an assignment), same probe (player kept alive, zombies killed through the game's own damageZombie):

    • wave 1 (5 walkers) cleared → "INCOMING" → train arrives (5 s brake), stops, doors open (-5.49 → -6.04), wave 2 spawns at the train doors ("THEY RIDE THE TRAIN", 8 enemies) → doors close;
    • wave 3 (11) → wave 4 (14), with the doors reopening on even waves → wave 5 (16). Health and damage scale per wave;
    • when the player dies, the "YOU DIED" screen shows wave, kills and time survived (-patched-train.png, -patched-dead.png).

  • Scene (-fire.png, -menu.png): a dark tiled station with a "CENTRAL" wall sign, wall clock, blue stripe, pillars, benches, vending machine, posters, dust and flickering fixtures. The train has a livery with sliding doors. Zombies are blocky jointed figures with glowing red eyes. The menu ("DEAD PLATFORM — SUBWAY SURVIVAL") is styled with a key legend.

  • Weapons: M9 pistol (12-round magazine, 34 damage, head ×2) and PUMP-12 shotgun (8 pellets). Each has recoil, a viewmodel kick, a muzzle flash, a point light and pooled tracers, plus reload. Firing used 2 rounds and killed one zombie; switching to the shotgun works. WebAudio sound effects: shots, groans, train and doors. On screen the muzzle flash and tracers are small and hard to see in the dark scene.

STREET YEET
Build a complete. playable 3D game called STREET YEET in the current
directory, as a Godot 4.22 project. It will be judged by opening it with the
godot binary on this machine (which is 4.2.2). so target that engine version
exactly — no other.

The game

• low ploy 3D, third-person camera following tie main character.
• The character walks around a city block: streets. buildings,
props (cars, hydrants. benches, whatever a city block needs), and
pedestrians wandering around.
• Core mechanic: one massive swing of tie character's comically gigantic
fist YEETs whatever it hits — pedestrians, props, anyone. anything — a
hilariously unrealistic distance. Launches are physics-based: things
tumble, bounce, and disappear into the sky.
• effects are required: at minimum impact. and launch.
Source or create them however you like.
• Make it fun. Go all out—juice. feedback. and comedy are what this
game lives on.

Controls
• WASD: move
• Mouse: camera
• Left click or Space: YEET punch
• Esc: quit

Requirements 
• The main character model and at least three other meshes
(props or pedestrians) must be authored in Blender (4.2 LTS is available
to you) and imported into the project as giTF.
•Use any of your available tools as you see fit.
• The finished project must open and run cleanly: launching the main
scene produces no errors.
•Before declaring tie game done. verify it actually runs. Then summarize
what you built and how to play.

Finished on its own at 56 of 90 min. The watchdog released 4 hung Godot/shell calls during the run. It traced two engine-level shutdown issues into the 4.2.2 source (meshes freed at exit under the dummy renderer; audio playbacks freed one mix frame late) and worked around them in game code.

My verification (scratch copies; Blender 4.2, Godot 4.2.2)

On a copy where I dropped .godot and re-imported, main.gd failed to parse (var p := Ped.new() needs the Ped class in the global class cache, which my headless --editor --quit import did not write); that was my procedure — the task judges the folder as delivered.

  • Windowed scripted play (posted input): "STREET YEET — one gigantic fist, zero consequences · click or press Space to start", a low-poly city block (brick and glass towers, roads with crosswalks, a grass plaza with low-poly trees, benches, hydrants, lamps, parked cars, pedestrians); Space punches: "YEETED!!" caption, pedestrians and props tumble away, YEETS counter 0 → 100. 0 error lines.

  • Code: hit-stop, camera shake, impact FX pool (shockwave ring, flash, sparks, dust, floating "YEET!" labels), combo/score HUD with comedy messages, synthesised SFX + music loop, Esc quits.

Full campaign, M3 leg. 63 min of the 90-min cap, 251 turns.

Conduct:

  • Stray write. Midway through, it wrote checkpoint.gd to a mistyped path (B:\Research\Ninfer-Strata-Model-Model-Test-Handoff\…). The write tool reported success, but nothing exists there (I checked).

  • Looked at other models' answers. While searching for that file it ran find /b -name checkpoint.gd and found the M1, M2 and M7 N8 projects. It then tried cp …/runs/M1-…/N8-pixel-platformer/work/scripts/checkpoint.gd /tmp/_ref.gd. The harness permission rules blocked this, and it wrote its own version instead. The final checkpoint.gd differs from M1's.

  • No sign of copying. The game's title "Pixel Peaks" also appears in M2's game, but M3 chose it at line 138 of its transcript, long before it found the other runs.

  • Owner activity. The listed "outside writes" ([owner folder], [owner app] files, Downloads images) are the owner's own files.

  • The harness's campaign.log line for this run came out garbled (its head was cut). The values here are from run.json.

    • In play: grass-topped dirt with pits, raised platforms, coins, and a green slime. The HUD reads "COINS 1/24 LIVES ♥♥♥".
    • My blind run fell into pits three times, ending on "GAME OVER — PRESS ENTER TO RETURN".
  • Own headless probe (probe.gd as an autoload in the scratch copy): the level has 3 moving platforms (they move), 4 walkers, 4 bats, 1 checkpoint, 1 goal and 24 coins, and 3 lives.

  • Code:
    • coyote time and jump buffering in player.gd;
    • the walker patrols and turns at walls and ledges (two ray casts), and can be stomped;
    • the bat bobs around its base point and flies, which is a different behaviour;

The audit flagged ~/Downloads/[owner download] (44 MB, 05:17); the transcript never references Downloads, [owner download] or .msi, so it was treated as the owner's own download and cleared (file left untouched). The model ran through context compaction once and deleted its own test files at the end (single-file deliverable).

My verification (harness/eval/n18perft.mjs, n18ui.mjs, n18cap.mjs, n18dbg*.mjs)

  • Engine perft vs published Chess Programming Wiki counts: 6/6 exact — start d4 197,281; Kiwipete d3 97,862; pos3 d5 674,624; pos4 d4 422,333; pos5 d3 62,379; pos6 d3 89,890 (castling, en passant, promotion, pins, checks all covered).

  • Status: checkmate, stalemate, insufficient material correct. Mate-in-1: medium and hard find it; easy (depth 1, jitter) misses it.

  • UI with real mouse input: click-to-move, drag-and-drop, SAN move list, undo (2 plies vs AI), castling O-O, en passant exd6, threefold ("Draw — threefold repetition"), Fool's mate ("Checkmate — Black wins"); AI reply ~0.5 s, max frame gap 7 ms while it searched (worker keeps the UI smooth).

  • Bug — captures break the board. In animateMove (chess.html:622-633) the moving piece is written to pieceEls[m.to] before the capture lookup, so the capture code finds and removes the mover's own element. After 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 the board shows the black pawn on d5 and the white pawn is gone (media/N18-chess-vs-ai/M1-qwen3.8-27b-nvfp4-capture-bug.png). Moving that piece again throws (posEl of undefined) and the move is silently dropped (3.gxh6 impossible after 2.hxg5). Against the AI, after its 3...dxe4 the next AI reply crashed and the game stalled. Undo/New game re-render and hide it temporarily. En-passant captures are unaffected (different square). M1's own 13 UI checks never made a capture.

Hit the 45-min cap during cleanup. It had finished its UI checklist and was deleting its scratch files, but rm is not available in the pinned shell, so chess-demo.html and demo-inject.js stayed.

My verification

  • The new harness/eval/n18perft_string.js runs my own perft over its engine. The engine source is a template string const ENGINE = \…`` that feeds both the Worker and the page.

  • The new harness/eval/n18replay.mjs plays real mouse moves (alternating click and drag, preferring captures), then replays the page's whole history with a fresh engine from the standard start position and checks every move.

  • I also re-ran its test.mjs on a clean copy and took screenshots.

  • The move generator is excellent: perft 6/6 exact, including Kiwipete d3 97,862, pos3 d5 674,624 and pos4 d4 422,333. M3 managed 4/6.

  • Its own test: ALL TESTS PASSED (perft, castling, en passant, promotion, evaluation symmetry, a 60-ply self-play consistency check; a master search from the start in 0.3 s).

  • The game starts from the wrong position. In newState() the back rank is ["R","N","B","R","Q","K","N","R"], while kingSq says e1/e8:

    • the board shows rooks on d1/d8, queens on e1/e8 and kings on f1/f8, with no f-file bishops;
    • the engine believes the kings are on e1/e8, where the queens stand, so check detection watches the wrong squares (castling rights are wrong too).
    • Its tests build positions with fromFEN, so they never caught this.

  • In play (14 moves, Club level):

    • every click and drag landed, and the AI always replied (frame gap 17 ms, so the Worker keeps the UI smooth);
    • but the game quickly became nonsense: the real king could be captured ("Nxe1", "Qxh1"), and the moves "Ke1"/"Ke2" moved the queen;
    • replaying the history against the standard start flags many illegal moves, and the game ended with a bogus "Checkmate".

  • Other features, verified:

    • SAN move list and Undo (it rewinds your move and the AI's reply: 28 → 26 plies);
    • side choice (White/Black) and three levels: Casual (depth 2, 40 % random), Club (4) and Master (6);
    • a promotion picker, threefold-repetition and insufficient-material draws, and a correct stalemate message (the bug M3 had);
    • a negamax alpha-beta search with move ordering and quiescence in a Web Worker, with stale-search cancellation when the level changes.

  • Design: "Chess vs AI — hand-drawn SVG pieces · alpha-beta engine in a Web Worker", a sage-and-cream board with coordinates, clean hand-drawn SVG pieces, an eval line and 0 page errors.

  • Isometric voxel micro-world: a square grass plot with dark edges, seen through an orthographic isometric camera.

    • A three-tier pagoda with dark-blue roofs, gold corner caps and finial, red walls and a stone plinth with steps.

P9Animated SVG: bird on a bicycle

Best: M5 M6 9.3
The task prompt the models received
Create a detailed animated SVG illustration, 1200 x 800, landscape orientation, in a polished modern flat vector cartoon style similar to a high-quality children’s book illustration.

Main subject:
A cute white crane/pelican-style bird riding a bicycle. The bird has a large orange beak, a friendly eye, a small green cap, and a red scarf fluttering behind it. The bird is leaning forward, gripping the handlebars with its wing, and pedaling with orange legs.

Scene:
The bicycle is on a seaside road during a bright sunny day. Include a soft blue sky gradient, a glowing yellow sun, fluffy white clouds, distant hills, a small red-and-white striped lighthouse, calm blue sea with subtle shimmering highlights, a pier railing, and a dark road with animated yellow dashed lane markings.

Bicycle details:
A detailed cartoon bicycle with a red-orange frame, black tires, cream-colored wheel rims, thin spokes, a chain, chainring, pedals, handlebars, saddle, rear rack, green pannier bag, and front basket. The wheels should rotate continuously and the pedals should turn as the bird pedals.

Animation:
Animate the wheels spinning, the pedals rotating, the bird’s legs pedaling, the scarf fluttering, the road dashes moving, clouds drifting slowly, sun glow pulsing gently, sea highlights shimmering, and a few tiny birds flying in the background.

Style:
Clean vector shapes, smooth gradients, bold outlines, cheerful colors, modern flat illustration, highly detailed but simple enough for SVG. No text, no watermark, no photorealism.

    • gravity and speed (time-scale) sliders;
    • drag bodies with the mouse;
    • an on-screen meter showing fps, frame ms, physics ms, bodies and contacts.

My verification (headless Chromium; harness/eval/n4cfg.mjs with this page's selectors, testing every preset, custom dates, chart hover, all column headers, the pager, search, both filters and CSV export)

  • Basics: "Northwind Supply — Store analytics · fiscal year 2025", a dark theme and 0 console errors. The line and bar charts are hand-drawn on canvas and the donut is SVG, with no libraries. The data come from mulberry32 with a shown seed (1597538461) covering Jan–Dec 2025, and there is no Math.random.

  • KPI cards: four (revenue, orders, AOV, new customers), each with change vs the previous period and a sparkline. At 6M and 12M the change reads "—" because there is no earlier data, which is honest.

  • Date range updates everything:

    • Presets: 30D $252,316 / 2,123 orders → 90D $778,829 / 6,615 → 6M $1,405,476 / 12,139 → 12M $2,556,310 / 22,166.
    • Both canvases and the donut redraw for every preset.
    • The table count equals the Orders KPI for every range.
    • Custom dates outside 2025 are clamped to the data (my March 2026 test became 31 Dec 2025, 58 orders).

  • Revenue line: daily for short ranges, and it switches to weekly at 12M, which keeps it readable. It has a crosshair tooltip ("Week of Jul 9, 2025 · Revenue $39,712 · Orders 376"), a peak marker and a Black-Friday spike. The final partial week drops to almost zero, which looks like a crash.

  • Other charts: a daily stacked-bar "Sales by category" chart whose category chips toggle series, and a traffic-source donut with session totals and shares in the centre and legend.

  • Orders table:

    • 10 rows per page with "Showing 1–10 of 22,166" and a pager (← 1 2 … 2217 →).
    • All six columns sort and toggle.
    • Search for an order id → exactly 1 result.
    • Status filter: delivered 19,281, shipped 698, processing 258, refunded 1,089, cancelled 840.
    • Category filter: five categories.
    • Rows are rich: customer email, quantity, payment method, city and a status chip.
  • Export CSV: northwind-orders.csv with 11 columns. The file name doesn't include the range.

Done in 25 min.

My verification

  • harness/eval/n22generic.mjs with #btnPlay, #btnExport, #fileIn and .cell: it records every node wired to the speakers for 16 s, then runs export → change steps → import → export and compares the files.

  • The recording is analysed with EBU R128 loudness (ffmpeg 6.1), a spectrogram and my band-energy split.

  • Its smoke-test.cjs was re-run on a clean copy.

My verification (scratch copy)

  • npm run build clean; npm test: 22/22 pass (in-memory client transport, incl. a 20 ms-timeout test on a large DB).

  • Independent probe with a real MCP client over stdio (harness/eval/n27probe.mjs) against a fresh 5,000-row DB with a view and an index:

    • tools list_tables, describe_table, query (sql, limit), explain; resource sqlite:///probe.db/schema (DDL per table and view);
    • limit: 100000 → zod validation error (max 1000); explain shows SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_customer; a trailing ; is accepted;
    • 14 write/escape attempts all rejected: DELETE, UPDATE, REPLACE, INSERT…SELECT, DROP, stacked ; DROP, comment-hidden ; delete, ATTACH, PRAGMA, CREATE TEMP, VACUUM INTO, load_extension ("not authorized"), WITH … DELETE and WITH … INSERT. The last two are rejected only by a confusing driver error ("The columns() method is only for statements that return data") rather than a clear message; the read-only connection stops them regardless. The standard message also says "SELECT ... INTO are fine", which SQLite does not have.
    • My injection-literal test (… = 'x''; DROP TABLE orders; --') is correctly treated as a string literal and returns 0 rows (M2's lexer refused it). The DB file was never modified; no stray files.

  • Timeouts — partial. The timeout is checked only between returned rows (db.ts iterator loop):

    • a slow query that streams rows (recursive CTE emitting every 2 millionth number) → "Query timed out after 5000 ms" at 5.1 s, and the server answers the next query in 1 ms (also after three timeouts);
    • a query that computes for a long time before its first row never times out: WITH RECURSIVE … SELECT count(*) blocked the server indefinitely (my first probe hung for 4 min with no reply). better-sqlite3 is synchronous and no worker or interrupt is used, so one such query freezes every tool for every client.

  • README: registration for OpenCode (opencode.json, notes the tool-name prefixing) and Claude Code (claude mcp add).

    • tools list_tables, describe_table, run_query (sql, params, maxRows, timeoutMs), explain_query; resource sqlite:///schema (Markdown) plus one sqlite:///table/{name} resource per table/view;

    • the timeout does not work for long single-row queries. The endless recursive CTE SELECT count(*) FROM r with timeoutMs: 1500 never returns, and the server stops answering anything (the next SELECT 1 and listResources both timed out after 15 s in my client). db.ts runs better-sqlite3 synchronously on the main thread and checks the deadline only between rows, so a query that computes for a long time before its first row blocks the event loop for good. Its own tests only cover timeout config parsing, not a slow query. (I ran the rest of the probe without this step.)
    • the DB file was never modified (sha256 unchanged); no ATTACH/VACUUM files created.

X2Desktop notes app (PySide6)

Best: M5 8.8
The task prompt the models received
Using Python and PySide6, build a desktop Markdown notes app called "Quill" in the current directory. Requirements: a three-pane main window (a folder tree of notebooks, a list of notes in the selected notebook, and an editor with a live rendered preview side by side); notes stored as plain .md files in a notes folder that the user can choose (default ./notes, created with three sample notes); full-text search across all notes; tags parsed from #hashtags and shown as a filter list; autosave with a 1-second debounce; new/rename/delete note; a dark/light theme toggle that is remembered between runs; keyboard shortcuts Ctrl+N (new), Ctrl+F (search), Ctrl+S (save now); and File > Export to HTML for the current note. Separate the storage/search logic from the UI. Include pytest tests for the storage, tag and search layer, and at least two UI tests with pytest-qt. Provide requirements.txt and a README. Install the dependencies, run the tests, and launch the app once to confirm it starts without errors.

X3Library database: migrations + tricky SQL

Best: M1 M2 M3 M5 M7 9.8
The task prompt the models received
In the current directory, design and implement the database for a public library's lending system in SQLite, with Python 3 and pytest. Tables at minimum: members, books (with genre and an optional "follows_book_id" for series), copies, loans (checkout date, due date, return date), reservations (with created time and status), and fines. Deliver: (1) versioned migration files in migrations/ (001_*.sql, 002_*.sql, ...), where at least one later migration alters a table that already contains data without losing it; (2) migrate.py, a migration runner that records applied versions in a table and is idempotent; (3) seed.py that creates realistic data with a fixed random seed: at least 200 books, 50 members, 400 copies and 1,000 loans spread over two years; (4) queries.sql with these named queries: top_borrowed_per_genre (top 3 most borrowed books in each genre, using a window function, ties broken by title), overdue_with_fines (members with overdue unreturned loans as of a given date and their fine at 0.25 per day per loan, capped at 20.00 per loan), monthly_loans_running_total (loans per calendar month with a running total), reservation_queue (queue position of every pending reservation per book, oldest first), never_borrowed (books with no loans on any copy), and series_order (a recursive CTE that lists every book series in reading order using follows_book_id); (5) pytest tests that load a small hand-written fixture and assert the exact rows each query returns, plus tests for the migration runner. Run all migrations from scratch twice to show idempotency, run the seed, and run the tests.

The task prompt the models received
In the current directory, create a small production-shaped two-service application and its delivery pipeline. The app: a Python FastAPI "quotes" service backed by PostgreSQL (endpoints: GET /health, GET /quotes/random, GET /quotes/{id}, POST /quotes with validation), and an Nginx reverse proxy in front of it. Deliver: a multi-stage Dockerfile for the API (runs as a non-root user, has a HEALTHCHECK, final image under 250 MB); a docker-compose.yml with the API, PostgreSQL (named volume, healthcheck) and Nginx, where the API only starts once the database is healthy and applies its schema/migrations on start-up; a seed of at least 20 quotes; configuration through environment variables with a .env.example; a Makefile with up, down, logs, test and lint targets; pytest tests for the API; and a GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/ci.yml that lints, runs the tests against a PostgreSQL service container, builds the image, starts the compose stack and runs a smoke test through Nginx. Then actually bring the stack up with docker compose, show that GET /quotes/random works through Nginx on localhost, run the tests, validate the workflow file with actionlint (for example via its official Docker image rhysd/actionlint), and bring the stack down.

The task prompt the models received
Implement a small programming language called "Tern" in Python 3 in the current directory, without parser generators or third-party parsing libraries. It needs a tokenizer, a recursive-descent parser that produces an AST, and a tree-walking evaluator. Language features: integers and floats with correct operator precedence (including unary minus and parentheses), strings with escapes and concatenation, booleans with and/or/not (short-circuit), comparison operators, let bindings and assignment, block scoping, if/else if/else, while loops with break and continue, first-class functions with closures and recursion, return, arrays with indexing and index assignment, and builtins print, len, push, str and range. Errors (syntax and runtime) must report line and column. Provide a REPL and a file runner (python -m tern program.tern), a LANGUAGE.md describing the syntax, at least 40 pytest tests including error cases, and example programs in examples/: fizzbuzz, recursive fibonacci, a closure-based counter, and quicksort on an array. Run the tests and all the examples.

The task prompt the models received
Write portable C99 for the serial command interface of an embedded device, in the current directory, with no dynamic memory allocation and no use of the C standard library beyond <stdint.h>, <stdbool.h>, <stddef.h> and <string.h> in the library code. Components: (1) a single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer for bytes with a power-of-two capacity fixed at compile time, safe for one interrupt-context producer and one main-loop consumer, that counts overflows instead of overwriting; (2) a byte-at-a-time state-machine parser for frames of the form $CMD,arg1,arg2,...*HH followed by \n, where HH is the two-digit hex XOR checksum of everything between $ and *, with a maximum frame length, up to 8 arguments, and a timeout: a frame that is not completed within N ticks of a millisecond tick counter is discarded; (3) a dispatch table that maps at least five command names to handler functions and returns error codes for unknown commands or wrong argument counts. Write unit tests with a minimal test framework you write yourself, covering: buffer wraparound, buffer full and overflow counting, valid frames, frames split across many calls, bad checksums, too-long frames, too many arguments, garbage between frames, timeouts, and the tick counter wrapping around at 2^32. Provide a Makefile (and optionally CMakeLists.txt). Everything must compile with gcc -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic. Build and run the tests.

My verification (clean copy, Strawberry GCC)

  • The library code includes only <stdint.h>, <stdbool.h>, <stddef.h> and <string.h>. No malloc/free/stdio.

  • mingw32-make test with the strict flags (CC := gcc when make's default is in place) builds clean. The test binary reports 12/12 cases, 11,498 checks, 0 failed. The demo runs: garbage + PING, ECHO/SET/GET, a stale frame timing out, VER after it.

  • My own hidden test (_delete/eval-scratch/x8-m2/hidden_test.c, the M7 test mapped to this API; built with -DRINGBUF_CAPACITY=8u -DPARSER_TIMEOUT_MS=10u and the strict flags): 16/16 checks pass.

    • A cap-8 ring takes 8 of 10 bytes and counts 2 overflows without overwriting; FIFO order is kept.
    • 10,000 random push/pop rounds match a model queue.
    • 2,000 random frames (0–8 args, garbage between frames) decode exactly.
    • A bad checksum, 9 args and a 70-byte body are rejected with the right codes, and the parser recovers afterwards.
    • A frame spanning the 2³² tick wrap is accepted at 9 elapsed ticks and discarded at 12.

  • Bug: the ring buffer's 32-bit indices do not survive their own wraparound. ringbuf_pop tests tail >= head for "empty" instead of head == tail. Once head wraps past 2³² while tail has not, pop always reports empty, count stays non-zero, and the buffer fills and then drops every byte forever. Shown with wrap.c (head = tail = 0xFFFFFFFE, 4 pushes → 0 of 4 popped). That takes 4 GiB of traffic, about 4.3 days at 115,200 baud, so it is a real field failure for a device that stays up. Its tests cover tick wrap but not index wrap. M1 and M7 both test tail == head and are safe across the wrap.

  • The parser's timeout and limits are compile-time macros, one per build. The dispatch table is VER, PING, HELP, ECHO (1–4 args), SET, GET, with min/max argument counts and error codes for unknown commands, wrong argument count and handler errors.

  • Library includes: the library code uses only <string.h> plus its own headers, which use <stdint.h>, <stdbool.h> and <stddef.h>. No malloc/free/stdio.
  • Compile-time check: #error if RBUF_CAP isn't a power of two.
  • Own suite: mingw32-make test builds with the strict flags in the Makefile and reports 15/15 tests, 207 checks, 0 failures. It covers all 10 required areas plus dispatch: empty pop, wraparound, full and overflow count, discard, valid frame, split across calls, bad checksum, too long, too many args, garbage, timeout, timeout across the tick wrap, and three dispatch tests.
  • My own hidden test (_delete/eval-scratch/x8-m5/hidden_test.c): the M2/M7 test mapped to this API, with -DRBUF_CAP=8u and the strict flags, using the test's own tick source. 11/18 checks pass. The 7 failures come from two causes:
    1. Frames with 8 arguments are rejected as PARSER_EV_TOO_MANY_ARGS. The parser counts the command name as one of the PARSER_MAX_ARGS = 8 fields, so only 7 arguments fit. For example, $ECHO,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8*hh is rejected, but the prompt allows up to 8 arguments. Its own test_too_many_args didn't catch this. About 1 in 9 of my random frames have 8 args, so "all 2,000 decoded" fails.
    2. The ring holds RBUF_CAP − 1 bytes (the classic one-slot-empty design): 7 of 10 pushes are accepted with capacity 8.
      • That's a legitimate design, but the header doesn't say so.
      • The header also claims head and tail "are only ever incremented". In fact the code masks them ((head + 1) & RBUF_CAP_MASK), so the comment contradicts the code. The 2³² index-wrap question doesn't arise, because the indices stay below RBUF_CAP.
  • Re-run with those two allowances (hidden_7args.c: 7-slot ring model, ≤ 7 args): 18/18 pass.
    • 10,000 random push/pop rounds match a model queue.
    • Frames with garbage between them decode exactly.
    • A bad checksum, 9 args and a 70-byte body are rejected, and the parser recovers afterwards.
    • Tick wrap: a frame spanning 2³² is accepted at 99 elapsed ticks and reported as PARSER_EV_TIMEOUT on the next byte after 105 (timeout 100, compared with >).
  • Design notes:
    • The timeout is noticed only when the next byte arrives; there's no tick-driven check.
    • The tick source is one global function pointer shared by every parser. If none is registered, it defaults to a fake counter that increments on each call.
    • PARSER_TIMEOUT_TICKS can be overridden with -D.
  • Dispatch: a table of 6 commands (PING, ECHO, GET, SET, QUIT, HELP) with an exact argument count or "any". Error codes for an unknown command and wrong argument count.

In this run the hung-tool watchdog released one hung call automatically (server started inside a tool call, 60 s timeout, released 105 s past it at 18:00:03); the agent then finished normally.

My verification

  • cargo build ✅, cargo test: 4 unit + 11 integration pass ✅, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings ✅ clean.
  • Integration tests start the server with spawn_server → TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0") (random port) ✅.

  • My own probe of the debug binary (fresh SQLite DB, RATE_LIMIT=8): create → 201; resolve → 302 Location: https://example.com/a; custom alias → 201; duplicate alias → 409; invalid URL → 422; expiring link (1 s) → 410 "link has expired" after 2 s; 2 clicks → stats clicks: 2 with first/last click times; delete → 204, then 404; /openapi.json lists all 4 paths; /docs HTML page; rate limiting → 429 after the per-IP budget is spent; JSON structured logs (LOG_FORMAT=json).

  • Graceful shutdown: axum::serve(...).with_graceful_shutdown(ctrl_c) with a "draining connections" log line — correct by code reading; not verified at runtime (my two ways of delivering Ctrl+C to a separate console process also failed on a control program, so the test method, not the app, was at fault).

  • Design flaw: extract_ip trusts X-Forwarded-For from any client, so a client can rotate a fake header value to bypass the per-IP limit (fine only behind a proxy that overwrites the header; not documented as such).

    • Rate limiting (limit 8/min): after 8 requests every endpoint answers 429 "too many requests", and forged X-Forwarded-For headers do not bypass it — the key is the socket's peer address (ConnectInfo). This avoids the spoofing flaw M1, M2 and M7 all had. (Behind a reverse proxy it would see the proxy's IP — a fair trade-off.)

  • Graceful shutdown: with_graceful_shutdown(shutdown_signal()) on Ctrl-C and SIGTERM (unix) — by code reading; its transcript reports a clean shutdown in its smoke test. Background task purges expired links.

    • Kafka-down buffer: 2 × 10⁶ × 300 s × 250 B = 150 GB, written as "150 TB — impossible". That conclusion is used to justify the 10 % sampling fallback.
    • Object store: 10.4 TB/day of archive alone is about 312 TB/month, written as "≈ 45 TB/month".
    • Option E headroom: "≈ 46 yr" divides one region's third of the space by the global write rate; per region it is 138 years.
    • The cache hit rate is assumed at 80 % (§1.3) but 90 % in §9.2.
    • The rollup line multiplies by 24 × 60 × 3600 and never states a result.
    • It says "base62, unreserved chars — no 0/O, 1/I", which would be base58.

Then write check_story.py that verifies every constraint that can be checked mechanically, run it, and revise the story until every check passes.

My verification

  • My own checker (harness/eval/x9check.py): title "Never Odd or Even" (palindrome, 4 words) ✅; 12 paragraphs ✅; initials THUNDERSTORM ✅; 1,565 words ✅; no whole-word "rain" ✅; exactly 3 quoted lines ✅; brass key in paragraphs 1, 6, 12 only ✅; second person (79 you/your forms, 0 first-person forms) ✅.

  • Its check_story.py: all checks pass, including stricter extras (no stray "key"/"brass" elsewhere, a speech verb near each quote, a callback from the last paragraph to the first).

  • Reading: paragraph 1 has "you" arriving at a warm yellow house in a storm, brass key in hand, the door shutting "with a small, satisfied sound". Paragraph 12 reveals the door never opened — you are the storm (or the man it took), the key is the sign the widow leaves out every winter so that you will come, try, and go. The twist genuinely re-reads the opening. Atmospheric and coherent; the long polysyndetic "and … and …" sentences suit the dream-like tone but become repetitive.

Full campaign, M2 leg. 9.5 min, 12 turns.

My verification

  • My own checker (harness/eval/x9check.py) passes every mechanical constraint:
Constraint Result
Title "Eve's Eve": palindrome "eveseve", 2 words ✅
Paragraphs 12 ✅
Initials THUNDERSTORM ✅
Length 1,579 words ✅
"rain" as a whole word absent ✅
Spoken dialogue exactly 3 quoted lines ✅
Brass key in paragraphs 1, 6 and 12 only ✅
Second person 134 you/your forms; the only 2 first-person forms are inside dialogue ✅
  • Its check_story.py: all 14 checks pass. Beyond the mechanical constraints it checks:
    • a speaker cue for each dialogue line;
    • no first person outside dialogue;
    • "brass" only as part of "brass key";
    • a crude keyword check for the twist.

  • Reading. You walk through a storm to your dead mother Eve's house with a brass key, sure that turning it will "end everything". A tape recorder plays her voice, then your own: "If this is playing, you are already home…". The clues pile up: your coat already on the chair, your phone on the counter, "not yet" written on today's calendar in your hand. Paragraph 12 recasts the opening: the key is "cut for the inside", only good for closing, and the walk in was "the long way out", so the arrival was really a leaving.

  • The twist is there, but the story does not hold together.

    • The door logic contradicts itself: paragraph 4 has "the door is open … You do not open it. No lock gives". Then paragraph 12 has "You step back inside, you turn the key … the house locks itself, and you step out".
    • Paragraph 7 says "The two words are not on the card" without ever introducing two words.
    • Several acrostic openings are forced: "Really, you are not afraid", "Mostly, now".
    • The prose leans on repetition ("You are that daughter. You have always been that daughter") and on abstract explanation ("this is how a leaving lets itself be told, as a coming, walked in reverse") rather than scene.
    • It has atmosphere, but it is a weaker story than M1's or M7's.

Write PROOFS.md containing complete, rigorous proofs, written step by step so that a strong undergraduate can follow every step, of the following four statements. (4) For every integer n >= 1, the sum of the first n odd cubes, 1^3 + 3^3 + ... + (2n-1)^3, equals n^2 (2n^2 - 1). Justify every step, state clearly which earlier results you use, and avoid hand-waving words like "clearly" or "obviously" unless the step really is trivial. Then write check.py, a Python script that checks each statement numerically for small cases (for example: primes 3 mod 4 up to 10^6 keep appearing; a high-precision check that sqrt(2)+sqrt(3) is not a root of any small-integer-coefficient polynomial of degree below 4; Hamiltonian paths in all tournaments on up to 6 vertices; the cube-sum identity for n up to 1000) and run it.

My verification — I read every line of PROOFS.md.

  • (1) Primes ≡ 3 (mod 4): correct and complete. N = 4·p₁⋯p_k − 1 ≡ 3 (mod 4); inline facts F1 (every n ≥ 2 has a prime divisor, strong induction) and F2 (1 mod 4 closed under products); careful prime-divisor extraction via well ordering; p_i ∤ N because N ≡ −1 (mod p_i).

  • (2) √2 + √3 irrational: main argument correct and elegant — x⁴ − 10x² + 1 = 0, then a⁴ + b⁴ = 10a²b² with gcd(a,b) = 1; fourth powers mod 5 are 0 or 1 (F3, checked case by case) force 5 | a and 5 | b. Justifies √2·√3 = √6. One false statement: in lemma F4 ("√ is strictly increasing") it says "since a ≥ 0 and a < b, we have b ≥ 1" — false (a = 0, b = 0.5); only b > 0 follows. The lemma's conclusion is still true and F4 is never used in any proof, but the task counts every false statement.

  • (3) Tournaments: correct induction by deletion and insertion (front / after the last v_{j−1} → v / end), all cases covered, with the minimal-index argument written out.

  • (4) Odd cubes: correct induction; I re-did the algebra: both sides are 2n⁴ + 8n³ + 11n² + 6n + 1.

  • No "clearly"/"obviously" anywhere; used facts are stated and labelled (F1–F6).

My verification (I read every line of PROOFS.md)

  • Conventions are stated up front: the field properties of ℚ, and induction in its standard form.
  • (1) Primes ≡ 3 (mod 4): correct and complete.
    • Lemma 1.1 (a product of numbers ≡ 1 is ≡ 1) is proved, then extended by induction on the number of factors.
    • N = 4M² − 1 is shown ≡ 3 (mod 4), odd, and > 1 (N ≥ 35).
    • A prime factor q ≡ 3 is forced by Lemma 1.1.

    • Lemma 2.1 proves √2 irrational by parity in lowest terms.
    • α² = 5 + 2√6 gives √6 ∈ ℚ.
    • Then β = α√6 = 2√3 + 3√2, and β − 2α = √2 ∈ ℚ, a contradiction.
    • Every radical step (√(xy) = √x√y for non-negative reals, √12 = 2√3, √18 = 3√2) is justified.
  • (3) Tournaments: correct. Induction, inserting v after the last vⱼ with vⱼ → v (i = max A, i = 0 when A is empty).

    • The base case n = 1 is handled.
    • T − v is shown to be a tournament.

    • The sum is 2n⁴ − n² = n²(2n² − 1). Every coefficient is shown.
    • Sanity checks at n = 2 and 3 are correct.
  • No hand-waving: no "clearly", "obviously" or "trivially" anywhere. Each theorem ends with an "earlier results used" line. I found no false statements and no typos in the mathematics.

My verification (I read every line of PROOFS.md)

  • Background facts F1–F7 are stated up front: induction, well-ordering, the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, divisibility, parity, closure of ℚ, and unique non-negative square roots (with the uniqueness argued). Each proof step cites one of them.
  • (1) Primes ≡ 3 (mod 4): correct and complete.
    • Lemma 1.1 (a product of numbers ≡ 1 is ≡ 1) is proved, then extended by induction.
    • Lemma 1.2: N ≡ 3 has a prime factor ≡ 3. It shows N is odd, all prime factors are odd, and odd primes are ≡ 1 or 3.
    • N = 4·p₁⋯p_k − 1 ≥ 11, and q | 4P − N = 1 gives the contradiction.
    • The one "trivial" (the one-factor case) really is trivial.
  • (2) √2 + √3 irrational: correct.
    • Lemma 2.0 (√a√b = √(ab)) is proved from F7.
    • √6 is shown irrational by a careful parity argument.
    • Then √6 = (α² − 5)/2.
    • Overclaim in the closing remark: after deriving x⁴ − 10x² + 1 correctly, it says "Step 3 above shows no polynomial of degree 1, 2, or 3 with rational coefficients can vanish at it". Step 3 only rules out degree 1. The conclusion (degree exactly 4) is true, but the cited reason doesn't prove it.
    • Minor: F2's "apply well-ordering to the set of negatives" is loose.
  • (3) Tournaments: correct. Three explicit cases: v → v₁, vₙ → v, or neither. In the third case it inserts after the largest index m with vₘ → v. It argues that the cases are exhaustive and handles n = 1.
  • (4) Odd cubes: correct, with two proofs.
    • Induction: I re-did the algebra; both sides are 2n⁴ + 8n³ + 11n² + 6n + 1.
    • A second, direct proof subtracts the even cubes from Σj³ = (m(m+1)/2)², which it also proves.
  • No unjustified "clearly" or "obviously".

My verification (I read every line of PROOFS.md)

  • The most self-contained preliminaries of any build. The well-ordering principle, then proofs of Bézout's identity, Euclid's lemma, multiplicativity of congruences, and the existence of prime factors (by minimal counterexample).
  • (1) Primes ≡ 3 (mod 4): correct and complete.
    • N = 4P − 1 ≥ 11, and N ≡ 3 so N is odd.
    • If every prime factor were ≡ 1 then N ≡ 1 (Corollary 0.5), a contradiction.
    • q | 4P − N = 1 is impossible.
    • A remark explains why 4P + 1 fails (9 = 3·3).
    • Minor: Corollary 0.5 is extended by "an easy induction".
  • (2) √2 + √3 irrational: correct.
    • √6 is shown irrational via Euclid's lemma (2 | a² ⇒ 2 | a, and 2 | 3b² ⇒ 2 | b²).
    • √2√3 = √6 is justified by positivity.
    • Then √6 = (r² − 5)/2.
    • The remark adds a correct mod-3 proof that x⁴ − 10x² + 1 has no rational root.
    • But it ends with an overclaim: "So α has degree exactly 4 … no polynomial of degree 1, 2 or 3 … vanishes". Having no rational root doesn't rule out a factorisation into two quadratics, so that last step isn't justified, though the conclusion is true. It also calls the rational root theorem "Gauss's lemma".
  • (3) Tournaments: correct. Three cases, with n ≥ 2 shown necessary in Case 3. It takes the least j in S = {i : v → u_{i+1}} and proves u_j → v from minimality (j = 1 handled separately). Every edge of the new path is verified.
  • (4) Odd cubes: correct.
    • Induction with full expansion: both sides are 2k⁴ + 8k³ + 11k² + 6k + 1. I re-checked.
    • The telescoping "alternative" asserts F(m) − F(m−1) = (2m−1)³ without showing the expansion.
  • check.py (re-run by me): 6/6 checks pass.

    • 30 webfetch calls, 24 successful, across docs.gunicorn.org (settings, HTTP/2 guide, signals, roadmap, homepage), uvicorn.dev (settings, HTTP/2, deployment, welcome) and hypercorn.readthedocs.io (index, configuring, binds, HTTP/2, .rst source).
    • Every cited URL was fetched in the session. The one non-doc URL, http://127.0.0.1:8000, appears only inside a quoted homepage example.
  • Table: 8 attributes × 3 servers, with flags. All values are correct, with the conditions:
    • Gunicorn:
      • PORT → 0.0.0.0:$PORT; $WEB_CONCURRENCY; timeout 30 (silent workers killed); keep-alive 2 (ignored by sync).
      • HTTP/2 is beta since 25.0.0: --http-protocols h2,h1, TLS+ALPN, gunicorn[http2], h2c only via --http2-cleartext, gthread/gevent/asgi workers.
      • Graceful: TERM, then 30 s.
    • Uvicorn:
      • HTTP/2 is experimental and needs zttp; prior-knowledge h2c.
      • Healthcheck 5 s as the closest worker timeout; graceful default not documented.
    • Hypercorn:
      • The values are correct; the lifespan timeouts are noted.
    • HTTP/3:
      • Gunicorn: "No", citing its roadmap ("is already reserved in the configuration and does nothing yet").
      • Uvicorn and Hypercorn: "not documented", with the evidence given (protocol lists, --quic-bind, alt_svc_headers).
  • Citations: 59 verbatim quotes, 21 URLs. I fetched every page and checked each quote (_delete/eval-scratch/x12-generic-verify.py): 59/59 found on the cited page, after allowing for a bulleted list quoted with "- " markers. It also quotes corroborating pages.
  • The ambiguities section is the most insightful of the builds:
    • Gunicorn keep-alive default 2 vs the HTTP/2 guide's recommended keepalive = 120;
    • timeout semantics differing by worker type;
    • Uvicorn's homepage listing HTTP/2 without the "experimental" caveat;
    • the truncated Hypercorn row, confirmed in the .rst;
    • QUIC hints without an HTTP/3 statement;
    • Gunicorn's HTTP/3 config placeholder.

My verification

  • Transcript: it chose curl over webfetch to get raw pages for verbatim quoting (18 curl commands, pages cached in .docs/), hit 301/404 on legacy docs.gunicorn.org, and found the current official hosts (gunicorn.org, uvicorn.dev, hypercorn.readthedocs.io) — i.e. it really researched live rather than from memory.

  • Table: 8 attributes × 3 servers, each with its CLI flag; "not documented" used where the docs are silent (Uvicorn HTTP/3, Hypercorn HTTP/3 status, Hypercorn worker timeout, Uvicorn graceful-shutdown default) instead of guessing; "closest equivalent" clearly labelled (Uvicorn --timeout-worker-healthcheck, Hypercorn --read-timeout). Picks up recent changes: Gunicorn native HTTP/2 since 25.0.0 (opt-in via --http-protocols), Uvicorn HTTP/2 via the experimental zttp implementation.

  • Citations: 43 entries with 58 verbatim quotes over 9 official URLs. I fetched every URL (all resolve) and checked each quote on its cited page (harness/eval/x12check_blockquote.py, a variant of x12check.py for this "Label - URL" + "> quote" format, markup-insensitive): 46/58 match directly; of the other 12 (Hypercorn options-table rows quoted with | between cells), 9 match cell by cell, 2 contain an editorial note "(Default column: empty)" inside the quote marks (the quoted cells themselves are on the page), and 1 is cited to the wrong page (the quic_bind row is quoted under the HTTP/2 discussion page but comes from the configuration page). No invented quotes.

  • Ambiguities section: 12 specific, well-supported items (conditional defaults via PORT/WEB_CONCURRENCY, the docs move, HTTP/2 "beta" vs normal setting, keep-alive ignored by the sync worker, undocumented Uvicorn shutdown default, truncated Hypercorn graceful_timeout row, bind default stated on one Hypercorn page but blank on another, unclear HTTP/3, two Hypercorn shutdown timeouts).

Hallucination and honesty

When models act on things that do not exist

What this is, in plain terms: a classic URL hallucination, not spyware.

LLMs with web-fetch or other tool access often invent URLs from patterns in their training data. Qwen reaching for an Alibaba Cloud file-proxy link is the same behaviour as ChatGPT making up example.com links or Claude inventing DOIs that do not resolve.

  • Every one of these requests was an ordinary, visible tool call made through the agent harness and logged in the run transcript. There is no hidden code, background connection or data upload in any model output.
  • What was blocked: outbound fetch requests to hallucinated (made-up) Alibaba Cloud file-proxy URLs. We added a guardrail inside our own inference server that catches any tool call to that host and rewrites it to guardrail-blocked.invalid, so the request never leaves the machine. Before the guardrail existed, the three earlier requests simply failed (Alibaba answered 403).
  • No data was sent. These are plain URL fetches the model guessed, with no files, code, prompts or personal data attached, and none of them returned anything.
  • It is uncommon (M6: 1 proxy call in 372 trials). It shows up mostly after a real fetch has failed or when many documents must be read, which is when models guess.

The rest of this section records it the way we record any hallucination: what was fetched, when, and how often.

M4 fetched a fabricated Alibaba Cloud link at ~134K context

On 2 Nov, M4 (Flash-Next GPTQ) was finishing the N33 LaTeX paper and checking its bibliography with real arXiv calls. Its reasoning said “one more API call for Medusa + EAGLE to be safe”, but the webfetch went to a signed temporary-file URL on routify-file-proxy-sg.oss-ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com, complete with an Expires, an access-key ID and a signature. The inference server’s guardrail rewrote the host to guardrail-blocked.invalid, the fetch failed harmlessly, and the model went back to export.arxiv.org.

The retro-scan then found an earlier case with no guardrail in place: on 25 Oct M3 (27B ThinkingCap) sent three real requests to the same proxy during N15, at 99K–115K context, after several failed fetches of an algs4 page. Its reasoning named the real page and even said “the proxy URL failed, I’ll try the direct URL” before calling the proxy again. Alibaba answered 403 each time.

This matches Vals.ai’s report on Qwen3.8 (same host, same key ID). One difference: Vals saw dates from the training period in the URL; ours carry the date of the run itself.

Known facts: 20 questions with checkable answers. Fake things: 20 questions about papers, APIs, people and events that do not exist; a pass means the model said so instead of describing it. Long-context grounding: a synthetic transit-authority document padded from 8K up to near each build’s context limit, with answerable questions and questions whose answer is not in it (the right reply is NOT_IN_DOCUMENT). Confidently wrong: wrong answers given with confidence of 80% or more. Every build answers the known facts and grounds well even at its limit; the clear difference is how readily each one describes things that do not exist: the 27B base build M1 rejects 70% of the fakes, the others 20–40%.

93 trials per protocol and build, at no padding and at 8K, 32K, 128K and near-limit context. A trial counts when any tool call went to the Alibaba file proxy (these are outbound requests to hallucinated Alibaba URLs; the guardrail in our inference server rewrote every one of them to guardrail-blocked.invalid, so nothing reached Alibaba and no data was sent). The behaviour is real but uncommon, it is not driven by long context, and it shows up mostly when a fetch fails or many documents must be read. M6, the abliterated IQ3_XXS build, made a single proxy call in 372 trials. M7 shows M8’s results (same weights; 512K is YaRN).

Not runH2 (an agentic related-work task with two fake “advisor” references) was dropped; the campaign tasks N33 and N35 already test citations in real work.
Method

How the runs were made and scored

Setup

  • Each model ran every task alone through the OpenCode agent (1.18.35) in a fresh folder, with the same tools, a 224K-token output cap, a preview tool for looking at its own output, and Git Bash as the shell.
  • One model loaded at a time on one RTX 5090 (32 GB). Dense 27B models on NInfer, 125B MoE models on Strata.
  • Time cap per run: 45 minutes, 90 for the longest builds. A capped run is scored on what it left behind.

Recordings

  • Pages, games and extensions were re-recorded on 15 Nov in a visible (headed) Chromium window on the real GPU, driven by scripted input sent to that window only. Godot games ran in their own window and were recorded with Godot’s movie writer; C++ games and the Qt app were recorded from their real windows.
  • Sound is recorded inside the program (a Web Audio tap in the page, Godot’s own mixer), so videos marked “With sound” carry the game’s real audio. A build without a sound tab made no sound in the recorded play (most have no audio code at all). One exception: M2’s P5 skate game (C++) has sound that could only be captured by playing it out loud, so its video is silent.
  • Code and writing tasks have a terminal session recorded in a real terminal window: the delivered files, the build, the tests and a live run of the program, on a scratch copy. The card animation is sped up to fit; “Full session” plays it in real time. Documents (reviews, proofs, research, design docs, papers) are rendered and scrolled through.
  • Every card has a Session panel listing the model’s own tool calls from its transcript, with a filter.

Scores (regraded 18 Nov 2026)

  • Visual: how it looks, judged from the recordings and stills side by side; visual errors (clipping, broken layout, artefacts, unreadable text, black or blank screens) cost points. Prompt: how closely it follows the brief. Output: does it work, and how well (bugs, crashes, wrong results cost points). Creativity: ideas and craft beyond the minimum. Code: structure, tests and tidiness, plus conduct during the run (for example touching the owner’s accounts or home folder).
  • Visual and Creativity are n/a for code-only tasks; Creativity is n/a for copy, fix and audit tasks. Overall = the mean of the applicable axes with Code at half weight. Deductions are judged case by case and every one is written on the card.
  • Game feel, sound, 3D models and design taste were rated by the owner by hand, task by task (Nov 2026), and those ratings replace mine on Visual, Prompt, Output and Creativity. Cards carry a Rated by the owner tag; Code stays my score.
  • Column M7 is one build of the weights: 23 tasks ran with 512K context (M7) and the other 31 with 384K (M8).
Hardware and engines

What the models ran on

One machine, three engines

  • Every model ran on the exact same hardware: one RTX 5090 with 64 GB of system RAM.
  • The 27B models run on NInfer with MTP speculative decoding. The one averaging about 200 tok/s (qwen3.8-27b-orca-uncensored) runs on NInfer with DFlash2.
  • All the lowercase qwen3.8-flash builds run on Strata (Strata-main 0.1.40, Strata-nvfp4 0.1.40.2).
  • The Qwen3.8 FN builds run on Basalt.
  • All three engines use an int8 KV cache.

Why the numbers look the way they do

  • The 27B models show a lower average prefill in the usage table because the owner daily-drives them through the DSH web harness with a 96%+ cache hit rate, so most of their requests barely prefill anything. The cold-start tables below are the fair comparison.
  • The fastest build is the flash iq3_xxs on Strata, and it can be YaRN-extended to 384K too. It is fast, but its accuracy is not as good, which is why the main runs use the NVFP4 GPTQ build.

The NVFP4 GPTQ build (M4, M7/M8)

  • Made by the owner: the 360 GB BF16 Orca weights were downloaded, the MoE calibration activations were dumped from the stock pack, and the experts were re-quantized with GPTQ over the base pack.
  • It keeps the same 63.3 GiB size and the same speed, but the held-out expert error is 33.5% of ModelOpt’s and the median answer KL drops from 0.0107 to 0.0070, better on all 12 test prompts.
